easy.heading: Starting Our Saturday Off Right
easy.body:
I started today by looking at that lonely cell at 0,0. It had a sum target of 6, and since it was the only cell in its region, I knew it had to be a 6. I looked at my pile of dominoes and found the 6,1 piece, which fit perfectly across 0,0 and 0,1. Even though 0,1 was marked as an empty region, the 1 from my domino just sits there quietly. It is a great way to get the first piece on the board.

Next, I turned my attention to the equals signs. I saw that cells 1,1 and 2,1 had to be the same, and cells 1,2 and 1,3 also had to match. By looking at the remaining pieces like the 5,3 and 0,2, I started fitting them into the corners. I placed the 4,6 domino so that the 6 landed at 1,3, which helped satisfy the sum of 5 at the bottom when paired with the other pieces. It felt like a little dance getting the numbers to line up just right, but once the 0,2 domino went into that 0,0 and 0,1 spot, everything else just clicked into place.

medium.heading: A Bit More To Chew On
medium.body:
This medium puzzle threw me for a loop at first with those less than symbols. I usually like the solid numbers of a sum, but here we had to be flexible. I looked at the bottom where cells 4,1 and 4,2 had a sum of 0. That meant both cells had to be 0! Since they were parts of two different dominoes, I had to find my pieces with zeros. I used the 1,0 domino and the 3,0 domino to fill those spots, which also helped me hit that big sum of 10 at 2,0 and 3,0.

The trickiest part was the middle where two different regions both needed a sum of 5. I ended up using the 2,3 and the 3,2 dominoes to bridge those gaps. It was a bit of a balancing act because the 2,3 domino had to satisfy the sum of 5 at 2,2 and 2,3 while also making sure its neighbor worked for the next region. I felt so satisfied when the last piece, the 5,5, finally found its home in that less than 7 region at 1,1 and 1,2. It really pays to start with those zeros at the bottom!

hard.heading: The Weekend Masterpiece
hard.body:
Wow, sixteen dominoes is a lot to keep track of! I felt like I needed another cup of coffee before tackling this one. I started where the numbers were biggest. That sum of 9 at 0,1 and 1,1 really limited my options, so I used the 5,4 domino there. Then I looked for the greater than 9 region at 0,5 and 1,5. Since there are only a few ways to get a sum higher than 9, I used the 5,6 domino to clear that area early on.

The breakthrough came in the bottom left corner. With a sum of 0 at 6,0 and a sum of 1 at 6,2, I could narrow down the 3,0 and 1,2 dominoes pretty quickly. I did hit a bit of a wall in the center trying to make the less than 4 constraints work at 2,4 and 3,4. I had to swap the 2,5 and 3,4 dominoes a couple of times before the math finally worked out for the surrounding regions. Once the middle was settled, the rest of the board, including those greater than 4 spots at the bottom right, just fell into place. It was a long journey, but finishing it felt amazing.

explanation.tips: Try to find regions with very small or very large sum targets first because they have the fewest possible combinations of dominoes. If you see a region with only one cell, that cell must be exactly the target number, which gives you a huge head start. Also, always keep an eye on your remaining domino pile so you don't try to use a number pair that you have already placed somewhere else.
explanation.learned: I learned today that the empty cells are much more important than they look. They do not have a math rule, but they act as a fixed anchor for whichever domino you choose to put there. I also realized that in the hard puzzles, the less than and greater than signs are actually more helpful than the sums sometimes, because they tell you exactly which high-value or low-value pieces to save for later.

faqs.question: How do you play the NYT Pips puzzle?
faqs.answer: In Pips, you place a set of dominoes onto a grid so that the numbers on the dominoes satisfy the rules in each colored region, such as sums, equalities, or inequalities.

faqs.question: What does the empty region mean in Pips?
faqs.answer: An empty region in Pips means there is no specific mathematical constraint for that cell, but it still must be covered by a part of a domino.

faqs.question: What is a sum target in Pips?
faqs.answer: A sum target is the number shown in a region that the pips in those specific cells must add up to once all dominoes are placed.

faqs.question: Are there any tips for the Hard Pips puzzle?
faqs.answer: Yes, focus on the regions with the most restrictive rules first, like very high sums or regions that only fit one specific domino from your list.
